blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Image-text corpora contain copies of one image, captions that describe one image in different ways, captions reused for different images, and captions that do not match their images. Each case calls for a different curation action. Deduplication and multimodal entity resolution (ER) only decide whether records are the same, and they are evaluated on labeled pairs. Yet pair scores do not tell which records end up in the same cluster or which useful captions get deleted. We therefore formulate image-text deduplication as graded multimodal ER, which decides visual identity, caption handling, and mismatches for each pair, and we evaluate it at three levels: pairs, clusters, and the retained set. Our method, VL-Dedup, groups records of the same visual entity into clusters and caps the size of each cluster. Within each cluster, a vision-language model (VLM) and CLIPScore decide which captions to keep and which to flag. We also build VL-DedupBench, with 50,000 COCO and SOP records and 66,788 labeled pairs. On it, a classifier that selects no false edge among the labeled pairs still joins millions of record pairs from different entities. Spending VLM calls on the pairs inside clusters, rather than on pairs with uncertain scores, gives better caption decisions from the same model. Even when almost all clusters are correct, keeping one record per cluster loses facts in many deletions, while the deletions of VL-Dedup lose much less information.

blocks.en:
Large image–text corpora support vision–language pretraining and retrieval.
Their quality depends in part on how corpus construction handles redundant or
contradictory records ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ; Gadre et al., 2023 ; Awadalla
et al., 2024 ) . Consider
the records in Figure 1 (a). A corpus contains copies of one
image, captions that add different facts about one image, captions reused
across different images, and captions that do not correctly describe their
images (mismatched captions). These relations call for different actions.
Copies of one visual entity can be deduplicated, captions with complementary
facts should be kept, and mismatched captions should be flagged for review.
A binary deduplication policy assigns the same action to all of them, so it
can join records of different entities or discard useful captions.

blocks.en:
Two lines of work address parts of this problem. Training data deduplication
removes near-duplicate and semantically redundant records ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Abbas et al., 2023 ) . It defines redundancy by surface or
embedding similarity, which does not tell whether two records show the same
visual entity. It is usually evaluated by removal rates or downstream
accuracy. Entity resolution (ER) decides whether records refer to the same
real-world entity using textual, visual, or fused evidence ( Fellegi and
Sunter, 1969 ; Elmagarmid et al., 2007 ; Li
et al., 2020 ; Wilke and Rahm, 2021 ) .
ER returns one identity decision per pair or one cluster per entity, which
does not say which captions to keep, and ER matchers are evaluated on labeled
pairs.

blocks.en:
A curation system makes its decisions in three steps. It decides pairs, it
groups records into clusters along the selected pairs, and it exports a
retained set of records. The user of the corpus sees only the retained set.
ER research has shown that clustering pair decisions changes the result ( Hassanzadeh et al., 2009 ; Menestrina et al., 2010 ) . Correct pair
decisions do not ensure correct clusters, and correct clusters do not ensure
a retained set that keeps every fact, so each level needs its own evaluation.
We therefore formulate image–text deduplication as graded multimodal
ER . Each pair receives a visual identity decision, a caption action, and a
mismatch action, and we evaluate the decisions on three levels: pairs,
clusters, and the retained set.

blocks.en:
We present VL-Dedup, a system for graded multimodal ER that separates visual
identity from caption and mismatch actions. A pair classifier scores
candidate pairs from visual and textual channels and selects edges. VL-Dedup
then adds three steps. (1) It groups records along the selected
edges into visual-entity clusters and limits each cluster to at most K K records, with K K chosen on validation data. (2) It combines the answer of a VLM about each
record with CLIPScore ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) into one record score, which sets mismatch actions.
(3) It asks the VLM for a verdict on the remaining pairs inside each cluster.
The verdicts set caption actions and do not change the clusters, so records
with complementary captions can share a cluster and still keep both
captions. An export policy turns all actions into a
retained set. Figure 2 shows the six stages of VL-Dedup. We
also build VL-DedupBench, a benchmark of COCO and SOP records on which all
three levels can be scored.

Figure 1 (b) shows four test records of VL-DedupBench. The
letter names the image, and the number names the record. A1 shows people
playing frisbee. A2 has the same image, but its caption, about a giraffe and a
zebra in a grassy field, comes from another image. B1 and B2 show that
giraffe, and B1 has the same caption as A2. A gradient boosting classifier
correctly selects no edge for the labeled pair A2–B1. It also selects the
unlabeled pairs A1–A2, whose records share an image, and A2–B2, whose captions
differ in one word. The selected edges are correct on every labeled pair, yet
the four records share a cluster, and further edges grow this cluster to
33,362 records. If the cluster held only these four records, an export that
keeps the record with the highest CLIPScore would keep A1 and delete B1 and
B2, so the giraffe scene would be lost.

blocks.en:
The example shows why VL-Dedup handles each level with its own decision. No
selected edge joins A1 and B1, yet they share a cluster through the path
A1–A2–B2–B1. One wrong edge, A2–B2, joins the two scenes, and every later
edge into either side extends the cluster. Over the whole test partition,
most false pairs of this classifier are joined by several such paths, so
removing single edges cannot separate them. The size cap limits all paths at
once, because no cluster can grow beyond K K records.
The record score targets records such as A2, which links the two scenes
because its caption describes another image. Inside each cluster, the VLM decides which
captions add facts, so the export keeps the records with complementary
captions instead of one record per cluster.

blocks.en: In summary, we make the following contributions.
blocks.zh: 总之,我们作出以下贡献。

blocks.en:
• We formulate image–text deduplication as graded multimodal ER and
define three evaluation levels: selected edges on labeled pairs, clusters over
all record pairs, and the coverage of deleted records by the retained set
(Section 3 ). • We present VL-Dedup, which separates visual identity from caption and
mismatch actions. It calls the VLM only inside clusters, where an export
decides what to delete, and its pair verdicts set caption actions without
changing the clusters. It flags mismatched captions with a record score that
puts CLIPScore and the probability of the VLM on one scale. With the size
cap, n n records need at most n ⁡ ( K − 1 ) / 2 n(K-1)/2 pair verdicts
(Section 4 ). • We build VL-DedupBench, with 50,000 COCO and SOP records, 66,788
labeled pairs, three edited versions of the test images, several photos of
each test product, and larger entities. We release it with the code of
VL-Dedup (Section 5 ). • We show that labeled pairs hide graph errors, even when they score
clusters. A gradient boosting classifier selects no false edge among the
labeled test pairs, and its co-membership F1 on these pairs is 0.9820. Over
all record pairs, its clusters join 7,711,852 pairs of different entities.
These errors spread along paths of edges, so the size cap repairs them better
than fixes to single edges. The cap lowers the false joins to 385, and over
eight settings it stays within 0.0051 of the best of five clustering
algorithms from ER (Section 6.2 ). • We show that results on the original records overstate robustness. A
classifier with only image features reaches F1 0.9997 on the original records
and 0 on Strong, the test images with the strongest edits. The cap repairs
the clusters of VL-Dedup on every test surface and on COCO and SOP corpora of
up to 580,767 records. On the pairs of SOP records with several photos per
product (product pairs), VL-Dedup reaches F1 0.2909, against 0.1658 for the
strongest baseline (Section 6.2 ). • We show that the same VLM judges single records better than pairs, and
that correct clusters still lose facts. For captions taken from other images
(swapped captions), the probability of the VLM for one record reaches F1
0.9264, and the combined record score reaches 0.9429, against 0.6549 for the
pair verdict. Inside clusters, the VLM also finds complementary captions with
higher precision and recall than on pairs with uncertain scores. In 50
sampled test clusters, keeping one record per cluster loses a fact in 70 to
141 of its 187 deletions. If it deleted 28 records at random, it would lose
10.5 to 21.1, against 5 to 15 for the 28 deletions of VL-Dedup. The ranges
span a strict and a lenient count of two AI auditors
(Sections 6.3 and 6.4 ).

blocks.en:
In this section, we review the work that VL-Dedup builds on and compares with:
data deduplication, captions and image–text consistency, entity resolution,
the clustering of pair decisions, and multimodal matching.

在本节中,我们回顾VL-Dedup在以下内容的基础上开展的工作,并与它们进行比较:
数据分解、标题和图像文本一致性、实体分辨率、
组合成对决定和多式联运匹配。

blocks.en:
Data management research treats the collection and cleaning of training data
as a data quality problem ( Whang
et al., 2023 ) . Training corpora
contain exact copies, near duplicates, and records that repeat the same
meaning. Hashing and n-gram overlap find repeated surface
forms at scale, and removing them reduces verbatim memorization ( Lee et al., 2022 ) . SemDeDup compares pretrained embeddings to find
records with similar meaning ( Abbas et al., 2023 ) . For images,
perceptual hashes find near-identical copies ( Zauner, 2010 ) ,
and copy detection embeddings also find copies after crops, rotations, and
color changes ( Pizzi
et al., 2022 ) . For image–text data,
LAION provides a corpus at web scale ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) , and
Webster et al. estimate that about 700 million images of its subset
LAION-2B are duplicates ( Webster
et al., 2023 ) . DataComp and MINT-1T study filtering and deduplication choices for multimodal
training data ( Gadre et al., 2023 ; Awadalla
et al., 2024 ) . Data-Juicer
packages data processing operators, including image deduplication ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , and SemHash uses compact embeddings for fast
semantic deduplication ( van Dongen and
Tulkens, 2026 ) . FairDeDup changes which
records SemDeDup keeps so that the pruned image–text data stays balanced
across sensitive concepts ( Slyman
et al., 2024 ) , and EcoDatum combines
several quality operators with a deduplication step to select image–text
training data ( Xu
et al., 2025 ) . These methods define redundancy by
similarity and report how many records they remove or how a model trained on
the result performs. They do not decide whether two records show the same
visual entity, and they do not keep a record for the facts that its caption
adds. VL-Dedup uses such hashes and embeddings to retrieve and score
candidate pairs, and our experiments compare it with Data-Juicer, SemHash,
SemDeDup, and caption MinHash.

Other work adds or rewrites captions instead of deleting records. LaCLIP
rewrites each caption with a language model and samples the original or a
rewritten caption in each training step ( Fan
et al., 2023 ) . VeCLIP and
Recap-DataComp-1B write new captions from the images with vision–language
models ( Lai et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , and DreamLIP samples several
sentences of one long caption as positive texts for an image ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) . These works train better models when an image has
more than one caption or a more detailed caption. Filtering methods score
each record instead. LAION keeps the records whose CLIP similarity passes a
threshold ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) , Data Filtering Networks learn the
filtering model ( Fang et al., 2024 ) , T-MARS masks the text inside each
image before it scores the image against its caption ( Maini et al., 2024 ) ,
and CAT filters noisy records before pretraining ( Radenovic
et al., 2023 ) . Other work checks whether a caption correctly
describes its image. SeeTRUE evaluates image–text alignment with human
judgments ( Yarom et al., 2023 ) , FineMatch detects and corrects mismatches
in specific aspects of a caption ( Hua et al., 2024 ) , and LVLM4CEC and
ContextGuard-LVLM use large vision–language models to check whether news
images and text are consistent ( Tahmasebi et al., 2025 ; Ma
et al., 2025 ) . These methods judge one
image and its caption at a time. VL-Dedup also scores each record in this way
to flag captions that do not correctly describe their images. Whether a
caption adds facts, however, depends on the other captions of the same visual
entity, so VL-Dedup decides it on the record pairs that share a cluster.

ER decides whether records refer to the same real-world entity. Classic work
treats matching as a decision under uncertainty ( Fellegi and
Sunter, 1969 ) and
splits the pipeline into blocking, similarity computation, and classification ( Elmagarmid et al., 2007 ; Christen, 2012 ; Konda et al., 2016 ) . Learned
matchers train neural pair models on labeled pairs ( Mudgal et al., 2018 ) or fine-tune pretrained language models on
serialized pairs ( Li
et al., 2020 ) . These matchers are evaluated by F1 on
labeled candidate pairs. Recent work uses large language models
for matching ( Narayan
et al., 2022 ; Peeters
et al., 2025 ; Fan
et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) and
for clustering ( Fu
et al., 2025 ) .

blocks.en:
Pair decisions become entities only after clustering. Hassanzadeh et al. compare clustering algorithms for duplicate detection, such as Center,
Merge-Center, and MCL, and show that the algorithm changes the result ( Hassanzadeh et al., 2009 ) . Draisbach et al. compare many algorithms
that turn pairwise duplicates into entity clusters and find that no single
algorithm is best in all settings ( Draisbach
et al., 2020 ) .
Menestrina et al. compare measures that score a predicted partition
against the true one, including pairwise F1 over all record pairs ( Menestrina et al., 2010 ) . Correlation clustering repairs inconsistent
pair decisions, and KwikCluster gives a simple approximation ( Ailon
et al., 2008 ) . Size constraints on
clusters appear in data clustering ( Zhu et al., 2010 ) and in
correlation clustering ( Puleo and
Milenkovic, 2015 ) . VL-Dedup uses such a
bound to stop paths of wrong edges, and our experiments compare it with
Center, Merge-Center, KwikCluster, MCL, and Louvain ( Blondel et al., 2008 ) . Other work uses transitivity to infer pair answers
and to save questions to a crowd or an oracle ( Wang
et al., 2013 ; Firmani
et al., 2016 ) , and noisy answers need extra
checks to avoid wrong merges ( Galhotra et al., 2018 ) . These answers decide
identity, so each answer can change the clusters. VL-Dedup asks a VLM only
about the record pairs that share a cluster, and its verdicts set caption
actions without changing the clusters.

Product matchers combine image and text representations to match offers
across shops ( Wilke and Rahm, 2021 ; Pollack
et al., 2024 ) , and an
industry pipeline combines compact multimodal projections with human review ( Tóth et al., 2024 ) . These systems decide product identity. Each
line of work above thus makes only part of the decisions of graded multimodal
ER. Deduplication removes records without deciding visual identity, work on
captions handles each record alone, and ER and multimodal matching decide only
identity. VL-Dedup gives each pair a visual identity decision, a caption
action, and a mismatch action. We know of no benchmark for image–text data
that scores clusters over all record pairs together with the coverage of
deleted records by the retained set. VL-DedupBench scores both, and the
labeled pairs, on the same records.

blocks.en:
We present the results of VL-Dedup on VL-DedupBench and on two full corpora
outside it. Section 6.2 scores visual identity on the labeled
pairs and over all record pairs. Section 6.3 scores caption
and mismatch actions on the labeled pairs inside clusters.
Section 6.4 scores the retained set, and
Section 6.5 measures cost and scale. We found the following.
(1) Labeled pairs hide graph errors, even when they score clusters. A
gradient boosting classifier selects no false edge among the labeled test
pairs, and its co-membership F1 on these pairs is 0.9820. Over all record
pairs, its clusters join 7,711,852 pairs of different entities, and pairwise
F1 is 0.0023.
(2) Graph errors spread along paths of edges, so a limit on cluster size
repairs them better than fixes to single edges. Removing one edge separates
only 147 of the 307 false joins of VL-Dedup without the cap. Over eight
settings, the cap stays within 0.0051 of the best of five clustering
algorithms from ER, while MCL falls up to 0.18 below the best and KwikCluster
up to 0.33.
(3) Results on the original records overstate robustness. A classifier with
only image features reaches F1 0.9997 on the original records and 0 on
Strong. A stricter edge threshold raises F1 on the original records to 0.9984
but lowers it to 0.1774 on product pairs.
(4) The same VLM judges single records better than pairs, and pairs inside
clusters better than pairs with uncertain scores. For swapped captions, its
probability for one record reaches F1 0.9264, against 0.6549 for its pair
verdict, and the combined score with CLIPScore reaches 0.9429. Inside
clusters, its caption actions gain 13.1 points of precision and 13.6 points
of recall. A pair with a verdict flag still holds a wrong caption 1.7 to 4.1
times as often as a pair that the VLM does not flag.
(5) Correct clusters still lose facts, and VL-Dedup loses fewer because it
chooses which records to delete, not only because it deletes fewer. Keeping
one record per cluster loses a fact in 70 to 141 of its 187 deletions. If it
deleted 28 records at random, it would lose 10.5 to 21.1 in expectation,
against 5 to 15 for the 28 deletions of VL-Dedup.

The VLM flags 306 same-entity test pairs above t t as mismatched. To
see how many of them hold a real error, we audit 59 of these pairs,
sampled by grade, and 60 control pairs above t t without such a verdict,
mixed and blind to the group. Two AI auditors, GPT-6.1-sol and
GPT-5.6-terra, label each caption as correct, locally wrong, or wholly wrong. The strict
count calls a caption wrong when both auditors flag it, and the lenient count
when either does. Under the strict count, 34% of the flagged pairs and 8%
of the control pairs hold a wrong caption. Under the lenient count, the
shares are 46% and 27%. A human check of the pairs on which the auditors
disagree gives 34% and 12%, inside this range. Of the 22 captions that both
auditors flag in the flagged group, 17 name a wrong object and 10 a wrong
location.

blocks.en: 6.4. Retained Set

blocks.en:
We sample 50 test clusters, 10 of 2–4 records and 40 of 5 records, 237
records in total, and compare two export policies. The first policy, keeping one record per cluster (keep-one), keeps the record of each cluster with the highest CLIPScore α \alpha and deletes the other 187. The export of VL-Dedup keeps 183 records, holds 26 for review, and
deletes 28. For every deleted record, the two AI auditors compare it with
the full retained set of its cluster. They see no policy, relation, or score.
The strict count calls a deleted record lost when both auditors find a fact
of its caption that no retained record states, and the lenient count when
either does.

blocks.en: 8. Conclusion
blocks.zh: 8. 结论

blocks.en:
We present VL-Dedup, a system for graded multimodal ER on image–text
corpora. It limits the size of each visual-entity cluster, asks a VLM about
the pairs inside clusters, and scores each record to flag swapped captions.
Our results show that correct pair decisions do not ensure correct clusters,
and correct clusters do not ensure a retained set that keeps every fact, so
each level needs its own evaluation. Labeled pairs hide graph errors even when
they score clusters, because the errors spread along paths of edges and join
records that no edge compares. Results on the original records overstate
robustness, so a benchmark also needs edited copies and several photos of one
product. The same VLM judges single records better than pairs, and pairs
inside clusters better than pairs with uncertain scores. The export of
VL-Dedup loses facts in far fewer deletions than keeping one record per
cluster, because it chooses which records to delete, not only because it
deletes fewer. We plan to train vision–language
models on the retained sets of different export policies and use the
downstream results to improve the export policy. In addition, we plan to
extend graded multimodal ER and its three evaluation levels to other curation
tasks, such as ER on text records with large language models and the
deduplication of interleaved image–text documents.
